record.context_brief: Fixed boundary set with unbounded complexity
record.original_question: Does there exist an integer N0 and an N0-tuple S of points in the Euclidean plane such that, for every N, there is a geodesic net whose set of unbalanced vertices is exactly S and whose number of balanced vertices is greater than N? Moreover, do such N0-tuples S form a subset of (R^2)^N0 of positive measure, or even a non-empty open subset?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 3.3.1. 1. There exist N0 and an N0-tuple S such that for each N there exists a geodesic net with S being its set of unbalanced vertices and the number of balanced vertices greater than N. 2. Furthermore, there exist not merely one such N0-tuple S but a subset of (R2 )N0 of positive measure (or even a non-empty open subset) of such N0-tuples.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Work in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. A geodesic net is a finite straight-line graph $G \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ (a finite set of vertices together with straight segments joining some pairs of them) in which each edge is a geodesic segment of $\mathbb{R}^2$. A vertex $v$ of $G$ is called balanced if the sum of the unit tangent vectors at $v$, taken along all edges of $G$ incident to $v$, equals the zero vector; otherwise $v$ is called unbalanced. For a positive integer $N_0$, an $N_0$-tuple $S = (p_1, \dots, p_{N_0}) \in (\mathbb{R}^2)^{N_0}$ is said to admit unboundedly complex balanced extensions if for every positive integer $N$ there exists a geodesic net $G$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose set of unbalanced vertices equals $\{p_1, \dots, p_{N_0}\}$ and whose number of balanced vertices exceeds $N$.

(a) Does there exist an integer $N_0 \ge 1$ and an $N_0$-tuple $S \in (\mathbb{R}^2)^{N_0}$ which admits unboundedly complex balanced extensions?

(b) If so, does the set of such $N_0$-tuples form a subset of $(\mathbb{R}^2)^{N_0}$ of positive Lebesgue measure, or even contain a non-empty open subset of $(\mathbb{R}^2)^{N_0}$?
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture appears to remain open. For three unbalanced vertices, it has been proved that there can be at most one balanced vertex, ruling out unbounded complexity in that case. For four unbalanced vertices, only finite constructions are known: an irreducible geodesic net with four boundary points and 25 balanced vertices was recently constructed (raising the prior record of 16), and this work is presented as progress toward, but not a proof of, the conjecture that arbitrarily many balanced vertices are achievable. The measure-theoretic / openness refinement (part 2) does not appear to be settled.

status_evidence.title: Towards Constructing Geodesic Nets with Four Boundary Vertices and an Increasing Number of Balanced Vertices
status_evidence.snippet: A geodesic net in the plane with four boundary vertices that has 25 balanced vertices and is irreducible was recently constructed, increasing the previously known maximum from 16 to 25.
status_evidence.claim: Recent partial progress: examples with 4 unbalanced and 25 balanced vertices, but unboundedness still conjectural.

status_evidence.title: Geodesic nets with three boundary vertices
status_evidence.snippet: A geodesic net with three boundary vertices in a non-positively curved plane has at most one balanced vertex.
status_evidence.claim: For N0 = 3 the conjecture fails; the open case concerns N0 >= 4.

status_evidence.title: Geodesic Nets: Some Examples and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Listed as Conjecture 3.3.1 among open problems on geodesic nets.
status_evidence.claim: The question is posed as an open conjecture.
